vignette:
Thomas is a 73-year-old American journalist who came to treatment after years of living as if danger might break through the next door at any moment. He is divorced and lives alone, and when he describes the event that divides his life into before and after, he does so with the strange detachment of someone recounting an assignment he once covered rather than something he survived himself. He says that is part of what troubles him most: the story feels so extreme that it is hard to believe it actually happened to him.

Years earlier, Thomas had been sent to report on a man-made disaster, arriving in the aftermath of a deliberate act that had torn through a public space and left scenes of destruction he had previously only described in print. As a journalist, he had moved toward the site with his camera, notebook, and the professional reflex to observe closely. He remembers the visual field first: twisted debris, scattered personal belongings, and later the photographs that circulated everywhere, freezing the ruined scene into iconic images. He also remembers an odd, sharply specific taste in his mouth during those hours, something metallic and chemical that became fused with the event itself. What remains with him is not a coherent account but a sequence that returns like film clips: the ruined setting, the shock of not knowing whether another blast or attack could come, the sense that anyone nearby might still be in danger. The unpredictability of those hours lodged in him as much as the horror did.

In the weeks afterward, Thomas tried to continue working. He told himself he had seen hard things before. Yet ordinary moments began to split open. If a related photo appeared in a newspaper archive, on television, or on a colleague's screen, he felt himself pulled out of the present. The memory did not come to him as a thought so much as a replay, vivid and repetitive, as though the same scene were projected again and again behind his eyes. At times, when he remembered it, he felt as if it were happening right now. He could taste that same flavor in his mouth and would go still, his body reacting before he had words for what was happening. He became wary of anything unpredictable-a sudden change in plans, an unexpected noise, a disruption in a routine assignment-because uncertainty itself felt charged.

As the years passed, his life narrowed around precautions that felt necessary to him. In restaurants, interview settings, and even at family gatherings, Thomas always chose a seat with his back to the wall so he could see the room. He scanned automatically for heavy lamps, letter openers, kitchen knives, anything that could be used as a weapon if something went wrong. At home, especially at night, he listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering. He knew, on one level, that his apartment was locked and quiet, but he could not relax in it. Safe places did not feel safe in his body. When something startled him or he felt threatened, he did not leap into action; instead he froze completely, as if stuck in place while his mind raced.

His work as a journalist gave him no easy refuge. Photo archives were part of the job, and newsroom conversation often turned to anniversaries, retrospectives, and familiar disaster images. He found reasons to pass those assignments to younger reporters, then felt ashamed of needing to. Over time his avoidance spread beyond work. He had come to believe that if he let himself really think about the event, he would not be able to handle it. So he pushed thoughts away, changed channels, closed browser windows, and steered conversations elsewhere. The costs accumulated quietly. He spent money impulsively-books he did not read, gadgets he did not need, expensive meals eaten alone-not because the purchases mattered, but because for a short while they interrupted the inner pressure. His apartment filled with unopened packages, a visible record of his attempts to comfort or distract himself.

What frightened Thomas now was not only the memory but what he believed it had done to him. He was certain that he would never feel normal emotions again. Pleasure, grief, tenderness, even simple interest in the world had flattened into something distant and unreliable. He said that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore, a painful statement for a man whose identity had once rested on bearing witness and making sense of events for other people. The divorce had preceded the trauma, but his solitary life made the emptiness more obvious; there was no one in the apartment to interrupt the long evenings of scanning, replaying, and waiting.

He finally sought help after freezing during what should have been a routine editorial meeting when an anniversary package brought related photos onto a conference room screen. A younger colleague had to take over while Thomas sat silent, tasting that old taste in his mouth and feeling for several moments as though he were back at the disaster site. He left humiliated and shaken. In coming to treatment, what he hopes for is modest but deeply felt: to sit in a room without mapping exits and weapons, to stop living as if unpredictability is the same as catastrophe, and to find out whether some part of his emotional life is still recoverable. What he fears most is that if he looks directly at what happened, he will come apart completely-and that the deadened, watchful life he has now may be all that remains.
